reason: The sources provide 14 well-documented claims supported by multiple sites, including specific dates, names, and the core irony of the colonial denial of African history.
story: Deep in the savanna of southeastern Zimbabwe stand the colossal granite walls of a medieval empire. Built between the 11th and 15th centuries by the Shona people, Great Zimbabwe was a thriving hub of global trade once home to nearly 20,000 residents. Its massive enclosures, built without a drop of mortar, reached heights of 36 feet. Yet when European explorers like Karl Mauch 'discovered' the ruins in 1871, they refused to believe that Africans had created such majesty. Mauch insisted the city was built by the biblical Queen of Sheba, mistaking local wood for Lebanese cedar. This racist delusion was weaponized by colonial leaders like Cecil Rhodes to justify land seizure. To maintain the lie, curators like Richard Nicklin Hall destroyed meters of archaeological layers, claiming to remove the 'filth' of African occupation. It was not until the 1920s that the truth was scientifically confirmed, finally restoring the city to its rightful builders.
angle: Colonial explorers refused to believe Africans built the massive stone city of Great Zimbabwe, instead insisting for decades it was a biblical replica of the Queen of Sheba’s palace.

claims.claim: The city's major construction period spanned from the 11th century to the 15th century.

evidence.quote: Major construction on the city began in the 11th century and continued until the 15th century.
structures that make up the ruins were likely built between the 11th and 15th century CE

claims.claim: The city was built by the ancestors of the Shona people.

evidence.quote: The edifices were erected by ancestors of the Shona people
scholars widely believed that Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona

claims.claim: The German explorer Karl Mauch first encountered and recorded the ruins in 1871.

evidence.quote: investigations of the site starting in 1871
Karl Mauch (first name sometimes spelled Carl) was a German explorer and geologist who was searching for gold and precious stones when he first encountered the ruins in 1871 CE.

claims.claim: Mauch incorrectly identified local wood at the site as Lebanese cedar.

evidence.quote: he concluded, the wood must be cedar from Lebanon
discovered some cedar beams that he assumed were from Lebanon.

claims.claim: Richard Nicklin Hall destroyed meters of archaeological deposits to remove what he called the filth of African occupation.

evidence.quote: discarding from three to 12 feet of stratified archeological deposits throughout Great Zimbabwe.
removed layers of sediment up to two metres deep throughout the site with the goal of removing “the filth and decadence of [African] occupation”

claims.claim: The Great Enclosure features granite walls that reach heights of 11 meters or 36 feet.

evidence.quote: walls as high as 11 m (36 ft)
soaring walls as tall as 11 meters (36 feet).

claims.claim: Archaeologist Gertrude Caton-Thompson scientifically confirmed the city's Bantu origins in 1929.

evidence.quote: findings were confirmed by another British archaeologist, Gertrude Caton-Thompson, in 1929
in 1929 Gertrude Caton-Thompson did the same.

claims.claim: Excavations revealed foreign trade goods including Persian pottery and Chinese porcelain.

evidence.quote: Glass beads and porcelain from China and Persia among other foreign artefacts were also found
uncovered a 14th century CE Arab coin, some 13th century CE Persian pottery and both porcelain and glass beads from China's Ming Dynasty.

claims.claim: The site contained eight iconic soapstone birds perched on pedestals.

evidence.quote: recovered from the monument are the eight Zimbabwe Birds.
The most famous artifacts are eight birds, carved out of soapstone.

claims.claim: The modern country was renamed Zimbabwe in 1980 in honor of the ruins.

evidence.quote: The nation adopted the name Zimbabwe in 1980
country of Zimbabwe--formerly Rhodesia, until its independence from England in 1980--was named for this site.

disputed: The exact peak population is disputed, with newer studies suggesting it did not exceed 10,000 while traditional estimates say 18,000 to 20,000.
The specific function of the Great Enclosure and its conical tower is debated, with theories ranging from a royal residence to a symbolic grain bin or ritual site.
The cause of the city's abandonment remains unclear, with possibilities including a salt shortage, environmental depletion, or a shift in gold trade routes.
